title: Four-year-olds starting school

turns.speaker: Wen
turns.text: My daughter starts formal lessons at four and a half. In Finland she wouldn't start until seven.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: And Finland does extremely well, which is the argument everyone reaches for.

turns.speaker: Sinead
turns.text: It's a weak argument on its own, though. Finland also has a different teaching profession, different inequality, different everything.

turns.speaker: Wen
turns.text: Sure, but the early starters don't hold their lead either. The gap between starting at four and starting at seven has gone by about eleven.

turns.speaker: Wen
turns.text: Close to it in reading. And the late starters tend to report enjoying it more, which matters over thirteen years.

turns.speaker: Sinead
turns.text: The part I find hardest to defend is the summer-born effect. A child born in August is nearly a year younger than one born in September and they're taught as if they're the same.

turns.speaker: Sinead
turns.text: That's a quarter of a lifetime's difference at that age, and it follows them for years.

turns.speaker: Wen
turns.text: Measurable into university entry in some studies.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: The honest counter is childcare. A later start means two more years of paying for somewhere for a four-year-old to be.

turns.speaker: Sinead
turns.text: Which is the actual reason the age is where it is, and nobody says so in an education white paper.

turns.speaker: Wen
turns.text: It would be a better debate if they did.

points: Formal schooling begins at four and a half locally, against seven in Finland.
Sinead warns the Finland comparison is weak in isolation because many other factors differ.
Wen notes early starters' advantage disappears by about age eleven, particularly in reading, and later starters report enjoying school more.
Sinead highlights the summer-born effect, where a child nearly a year younger is taught as an equal, with consequences measurable into secondary school and beyond.
Ben raises childcare cost as the honest counter-argument to a later start.
They agree childcare is the real driver of the current age, though it is absent from education policy documents.
